title: Tibet, 1950–1959
hook: Chinese forces entered Tibet; the Dalai Lama left for India, and others followed him into exile

segments.voice: Yesterday, Myanmar: monks who walked for their people, and monks who stood against hatred spoken in the robe's name. Your line: the robe for peace. Did a hateful word cross your path, and what did you do with it? Day one thousand thirty-seven.

What would you carry if you had to leave home at night, on foot, over mountains, and you didn't know when you'd come back? A coat. Water. A photograph, maybe. Some Tibetan families who crossed into India and Nepal speak of carrying something else too: a text wrapped in cloth, a small image of the Buddha, a string of prayer beads, a teacher walking a few steps ahead. Today's history isn't one night. It's a long exile, and the practice that went with it.
screen: `WHAT WOULD YOU CARRY?` → `A TEXT WRAPPED IN CLOTH.` → `A LONG EXILE.`

segments.voice: In the years named in today's title, Chinese forces entered Tibet, and Tibet came under the government in Beijing. The Chinese government and Tibetans in exile tell those years very differently, and this lesson won't settle that argument. What it can tell is what happened to a community of practice. After unrest in Lhasa, the Dalai Lama, whom Tibetan Buddhists hold as a great teacher, left for India. Others followed, monks and nuns and lay families, walking through high passes. In India, with very little, the exiles rebuilt. Monasteries with the old names rose again in new places, so that a monastery from Tibet might now stand in the hot plains of southern India. Schools taught Tibetan children their language and their texts. Debate courtyards filled again with monks clapping their hands as they argued a point, just as their teachers had. And in his public teaching from exile, the Dalai Lama has returned again and again to compassion, including for those he disagrees with, and he has said that an opponent can be your teacher of patience. The Pali word for that patience is khanti, and the Dhammapada sets it very high. In Max Müller's translation: "The Awakened call patience the highest penance." Patience here doesn't mean pretending nothing happened. Exile still hurts. Homes are still missed. Patience is what lets a person keep the grief without letting it harden into hate, and keep teaching while they wait.
screen: `CHINESE FORCES ENTER TIBET.` · `THE DALAI LAMA LEAVES FOR INDIA.` · `MONASTERIES REBUILT IN EXILE.` · then, large: `PATIENCE, THE HIGHEST PENANCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: hold refugees in metta, loving-kindness. Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. First, bring to mind anyone who has had to leave home: Tibetan families, or refugees from anywhere, or someone you know. You don't need faces; a sense of them is enough. With each out-breath, let a simple wish go toward them, in words that feel true to you: may you be safe, may you find a home. If the mind drifts to the news or to blame, notice that, and come back to the wish. Last, widen it to everyone caught up in that history, on every side. The bell holds the time.
Tibet. The high land whose teachers and families carried their practice into exile, and rebuilt it, monastery by monastery, far from home. Today's word.
Your line: the long exile. Today, when you walk through your own front door, pause on the threshold for one breath and remember someone who can't walk through theirs. Day one thousand thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists in exile keep their practice in rebuilt monasteries, schools and community centers, and some hold Tibet and all who suffered in their daily prayers and loving-kindness practice.

notes: Audit (2026-10-01): Dhammapada 197 ('not hating those who hate us') was day 1035's verse, quote and myth two days earlier; replaced with Dhammapada 184 (Müller: 'The Awakened call patience the highest penance'), which ties to the khanti original. Sweeping 'the teaching that came out of exile was not mainly about anger' narrowed to the Dalai Lama's own public teaching. Match, myth, screen and trapdoor updated. Keeper: confirm Müller's wording of 184.

Editor pass: Chinese rule line reworded to 'came under the government in Beijing' (less contested); stock lines 'something remarkable' and 'the part that surprises people' cut; hook's exile account softened to 'some families'; original changed from metta (used on day 1035) to khanti, patience.
The teaser hook field is reworded from the index hook to drop dates and counts (claims rule); the index itself is unchanged.

Politically sensitive: the script deliberately says the Chinese government and Tibetans in exile tell these years differently and avoids words like invasion or liberation. Keeper and owner should confirm this framing.
No dates or counts are spoken (the index title carries the years). 'After unrest in Lhasa' compresses the 1959 uprising; confirm.
Monasteries re-founded in South India with their Tibetan names (e.g. Sera, Drepung, Ganden in Karnataka) and debate courtyards with hand claps: confirm the general phrasing.
'Whom Tibetan Buddhists hold as a great teacher' is a deliberately modest description of the Dalai Lama; confirm acceptable.
The 'enemy as teacher of patience' theme is paraphrased from the Dalai Lama's public talks (it also echoes Shantideva); no quotation.
The metta wish in the practice ('may you be safe, may you find a home') is offered in the listener's own words as a loving-kindness wish, not a prayer; confirm acceptable.
The hook's items carried into exile are general images, not a sourced account; confirm they are fair.
